Black-faced antbirds (Myrmoborus myotherinus) exhibit a distinctive life-history strategy shaped by their understory insectivorous habits in humid Amazonian forests. Incubation is performed by both parents, and the developing altricial nestling remains dependent on parental provisioning for a considerable period. Under the thermal conditions typical of the nest microclimate (34.0 °C [T = 34.0 °C]), the age at hatching is approximately 16 days [ab = approximately 16 days], a value that aligns closely with incubation durations documented for several congeners in the genus Cercomacroides. This extended incubation period is associated with the relatively small clutch size and the considerable investment each egg represents. At the moment of hatching, the wet weight of the neonate is approximately 2.8 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.8 grams], a modest mass that reflects the altricial state of the chick and its dependence on yolk reserves during the first days post-hatching. The chick is initially brooded intensively, with both parents sharing thermoregulatory duties, before the rapid growth phase characteristic of nestling thamnophilids commences.

Following hatching, the nestling progresses through a rapid phase of somatic growth, during which adult body mass is approached prior to fledging. The ultimate wet weight for adult females in this species is 18.8 grams [Wwi = 18.8 grams], a value consistent with body masses reported for other understory insectivorous antbirds of similar size. This adult mass is achieved after a predictable developmental trajectory within the nest. The nestling period culminates in fledging, which occurs at 13 days after hatching [tx = 13 days after hatching] under standard thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a temperature that corresponds to the elevated metabolic rate of the active nestling during its final growth phase. This fledging age is relatively brief compared with some larger thamnophilids, reflecting the selective pressure for rapid departure from a vulnerable nest site in a predator-rich environment. After leaving the nest, the fledgling remains dependent on its parents for food for several additional weeks, gradually refining its foraging skills in the dense understory.

The transition to reproductive independence involves a series of well-defined developmental milestones. Under thermal conditions typical of active periods (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]), the time from birth to the attainment of reproductive maturity, or puberty, is 45 days [tp = 45 days]. This relatively short interval to sexual maturation likely reflects the high mortality rates experienced by young birds in Neotropical forests, favoring early reproductive capability as a means of maximizing lifetime fitness. Following puberty, individuals typically delay their first successful nesting attempt. The maximum lifespan recorded for the Black-faced antbird, under the same standard temperature regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], is 2,993 days [am = 2,993 days], equivalent to approximately 8.2 years. This longevity is notable for a bird of its modest body mass and suggests a relatively low extrinsic mortality rate once individuals have established a stable territory in a structurally complex forest habitat. The reproductive output of this species, when examined over the course of a year, reveals a modest but sustained strategy. Females typically lay a clutch of two eggs [N_R_i = a clutch of two eggs], and field observations indicate that they can produce one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year] during optimal conditions, yielding a maximum reproduction rate of approximately 2 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 2 eggs per year]. This annual reproductive effort is characteristic of tropical insectivorous birds that face high nest predation rates and invest considerable energy in each offspring through extended biparental care.

Basal metabolic rate measurements, obtained from respirometry trials on rested, post-absorptive individuals, provide further insight into the energetic physiology of this species. The maximum basal metabolic rate recorded for Black-faced antbirds is 50.91 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 50.91 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value determined at an ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This elevated metabolic rate reflects the high energetic demands of maintaining a stable body temperature in a warm, humid environment where thermoregulatory costs are not negligible. Interestingly, the combination of a moderate adult body mass of 18.8 grams [Wwi = 18.8 grams] and a relatively high mass-specific metabolic rate positions this species within the spectrum of insectivorous passerines that sustain active foraging throughout the day. Future comparative studies examining metabolic scaling relationships within the Thamnophilidae would help clarify whether this metabolic profile represents a conserved trait or an adaptation to the specific microclimatic conditions of the Amazonian understory.
